activity: to use a primary source like a settler's diary to explain why people moved west in the 1800s
knowledge_domain: to use a primary source like a settler's diary to explain why people moved west in the 1800s
fact: Gold was discovered at Sutter's Mill in California in January 1848, starting the California Gold Rush that drew people west in huge numbers.
story:
The war memorial in Middleton Park held forty-one names, and Rachel had walked past it a hundred times without reading a single one. Today she read all of them, because Mr. Gauthier had assigned a project: use a primary source, a real document from the time, to explain why people moved west in the 1800s. A diary counted. A textbook did not. The problem was that Rachel didn't have a diary yet, and the project was due Thursday.

"Look at this," Rania said, pointing at the smallest name on the bronze plaque. "E. Whitlock, died 1852. That's all we get. One letter and a year." Rania wanted the project to be about a person, a real one, not just a trend. She had already decided that.

Mr. Gauthier, who was tidying the memorial's flower bed nearby, stood up and brushed dirt off his knees. "The historical society has Whitlock's diary," he said. "His granddaughter donated it. You two can look at a photocopy in the library after school." He didn't say another word about it, which Rachel thought was very like him.

In the library, Brayden turned the pages carefully, like they might crumble even as a photocopy. Halfway through, he stopped. "Listen to this. He wrote it in the spring: 'Josiah talks of nothing but the gold struck at Sutter's Mill in California this January past, and says we should turn toward it.'" Brayden frowned. "Wait. Gold was discovered at Sutter's Mill in California in January 1848. That's the Gold Rush. That's what started it." He looked up. "So some of these people weren't going west for farmland at all. They were going for money."

Rachel felt something click, the way a puzzle piece does when you stop forcing it. She had assumed everyone packed up and left home for land, because that was the story she already had in her head. But the diary said otherwise. "So there wasn't just one reason," she said slowly. "There were layers. Some wanted farms. Some wanted gold." Could her whole family have come for one reason and the neighbor for another? She turned back to the first pages, hunting for evidence, and found it: before the news arrived, the diary was all about acres and soil. After, the word "gold" appeared eleven times.

Mr. Gauthier had warned them the class might participate in a discussion where anyone's theory could fall apart, so Rachel tested hers out loud. "If his town had a recession, farms failing, that would push people out. And gold would pull them. Push and pull together." Rania copied the line about Josiah onto an index card and smiled. "And E. Whitlock gets his name in our project. One letter and a year, but a whole voice behind it."

Rachel looked at the last entry, written in a cramped, tired hand, and read it aloud: "'We turn west tomorrow, and I am terrified and glad.'"

activity: to spot foreshadowing and symbolism in a short story and explain what they suggest
knowledge_domain: to spot foreshadowing and symbolism in a short story and explain what they suggest
fact: In James Hurst's 1960 story The Scarlet Ibis, a storm-blown red bird dies in the family garden, foreshadowing the fate of the fragile boy Doodle.
story:
Stella spread her homework across her grandmother's kitchen table: the short story packet, two pencils, and a worksheet that read "Find the foreshadowing. Explain what it suggests." She had read the story twice, and she still could not see whatever invisible thing her teacher wanted her to find. Her grandmother set down a plate of lemon squares and peered at the page.

"The Scarlet Ibis," Stella read aloud. "It's by James Hurst, from 1960. We have to figure out why the writer put a bird in it." Tatum and Johnny were coming over to collaborate on the assignment, and Stella wanted at least one idea before they arrived, so she would not look like the one who had nothing.

When they got there, Johnny dropped his backpack on a chair and announced his real plan. "I say we split the worksheet, each take a third, and copy answers. That's faster." Tatum shook her head. "Mr. Hoang will know. He's notorious for calling on people to explain their own answers out loud." Johnny groaned, but he sat down anyway.

Stella flipped back to the page where a storm blew a red bird into the family's garden. "Here. The scarlet ibis. It's exhausted, and it dies right there in the yard." She frowned. "Why would the writer give a whole page to a bird that just shows up and dies?" Tatum tapped the next paragraph, where the fragile boy, Doodle, was described. Stella read it slowly, and something clicked into place like a door. "Wait. The bird is broken and far from home. And Doodle is fragile too." She tested her idea out loud. "Maybe the bird is a hint. A warning planted early, so that when something happens to Doodle a few pages later, we should have seen it coming." Johnny flipped ahead, then went quiet. "Oh," he said. "Oh, no. Doodle."

"That's it," Tatum said. "It's like the bird's death foreshadows Doodle's fate." Johnny, who ten minutes ago had wanted to copy answers, was now scribbling notes of his own. "So when we write it up, we say the bird suggests what's coming for Doodle, because the story set them up like mirrors." Stella grinned and started her paragraph, and outside the window a crow landed in her grandmother's flower bed, startling them all. "If that crow dies," Johnny said, "I'm checking on Tatum first."

activity: to build a spreadsheet with a formula that adds a column and makes a bar chart
knowledge_domain: to build a spreadsheet with a formula that adds a column and makes a bar chart
fact: Every formula in Excel or Google Sheets begins with an equals sign; without it, the cell just shows what was typed as text.
story:
The summer Matthew turned thirteen, his grandfather's pill bottles began taking over the kitchen counter at the lake house, and Matthew decided to do something about it. Grandpa tracked his prescriptions in a bent spiral notebook, adding up costs with a pencil stub, and every month he worried he'd made a mistake. "I'm too lethargic in this heat to fight with numbers," Grandpa said one morning, fanning himself with a pharmacy receipt. "I just take the total they give me and hope."

Matthew had a laptop from school and half a memory of a computer lesson. He set it up on the porch table, opened a blank spreadsheet, and typed Grandpa's medicines into column A and their monthly costs into column B, ten rows of them. Then, in the cell below, he typed what he thought was the right thing: SUM(B2:B10). He pressed Enter, expecting a total.

The cell showed SUM(B2:B10), exactly as he'd typed it. No number, no answer, just the words sitting there like a nameplate. He deleted it and typed it again, slower, as if the computer might have misheard him. Same result. He sat back, and a wasp droned past his ear while the porch boards cooked in the sun.

He texted Dhruv, who had done the unit properly.

"It typed my formula but it just shows the words," Matthew wrote. His thumbs were sweaty and the phone screen blurred when he tilted it toward the light.

"Show me exactly what's in the cell," Dhruv replied.

"SUM(B2:B10). That's it."

"Every formula in Excel or Google Sheets begins with an equals sign," Dhruv sent back, and Matthew could almost hear him saying it in that flat, obvious tone, like he was reminding Matthew that water was wet. "Without it, the cell just shows what you typed as text."

Matthew stared at the little screen. An equals sign. He typed =SUM(B2:B10) and hit Enter, and the number appeared, right there in the cell: the whole month of Grandpa's medicines, added up in an instant. He laughed out loud at his own reflection in the laptop lid.

He didn't stop there. He made a second sheet for the year, then clicked through the menus until he found the chart button and turned the column of costs into a bar chart. Twelve bars, one for each month, and the tall ones in winter stood out like fence posts. Grandpa leaned over his shoulder, smelling of coffee and bug spray, and tapped the screen.

"Look at that. January and February are the expensive months." He rubbed his chin. "I'd never have noticed that in the notebook. The numbers just went round and round like they were in orbit."

"I can do it again next month," Matthew said. "You just tell me the prices and I'll put them in."

Grandpa grinned and shook the pill bottle nearest his elbow, listening to it rattle. "Then let's get to work, kid. We've got receipts in the drawer, and I want to see that bar for March."

activity: going to a first school dance
knowledge_domain: going to a first school dance
fact: The U.S. agency NIOSH recommends limiting exposure to 85 decibels to eight hours a day, and each 3-decibel increase halves the safe listening time.
story:
Isaac stood outside the gym doors with his tie stuffed in his pocket, listening to the bass thump through the wall like a giant's heartbeat. "You're going to commute back and forth in front of these doors all night, or are you actually going in?" asked Josue, who had already been in twice and come out twice, once for water and once, he claimed, because a slow song had started and he had "an emergency in his ankle."

They went in together. The gym had been transformed by streamers and one disco ball that mostly hung there, but the biggest change was the sound. Two speakers taller than Ms. Adebayo stood on either side of the DJ table, and the music didn't just play, it pushed. Ashlyn waved them over to a spot right beside one of the towers, and Isaac shouted his hello because at that distance, talking felt optional anyway.

After two songs, Isaac noticed something odd. His ears didn't hurt exactly, but they felt fuzzy, like they were wearing tiny sweaters. Josue kept yelling "WHAT" at people who hadn't said anything. Isaac leaned toward Ashlyn and said, "My ears feel weird. Like static." She shrugged and said that was just what loud was, and whether loud felt weird was subjective anyway, so his ears could be dramatic if they wanted.

Isaac wasn't sure about that. He remembered a safety poster in the nurse's office, mostly because it had a cartoon ear wearing a hard hat. It said something about eighty-five decibels being safe for eight hours a day, which sounded like a lot. But it also said every three more decibels cut the safe time in half. He did the math in his head while pretending to dance, which looked a lot like swaying with a headache. Eighty-five for eight hours. Eighty-eight, four hours. Ninety-one, two. Somewhere up in the hundreds, where the speakers probably lived, the safe time shrank to minutes.

"Okay, theory," he announced. "The fuzziness means we're cooking our ears. Test: we move." He herded Josue and Ashlyn to the far wall, past the punch bowl, near the exit sign. The music was still huge, but his ears stopped feeling like they needed a nap. Josue said "WHAT" one more time out of habit, then heard himself and cracked up. "It's the anecdote of the year," Ashlyn said. "Two boys defeated by a speaker."

"You didn't move until I made you," said Isaac.

"I was gathering data."

Ms. Adebayo passed by on hall duty and tapped the speaker tower on her way past it. "Careful near these," she said, and kept walking, and Isaac felt extremely smug, as if his theory had just gotten a stamp of official approval.

From the far wall they could still see everything: the disco ball finally spinning, Josue attempting a move he would regret, the punch bowl glinting orange under the lights. When the next song started, Isaac cupped his hands around his mouth and hollered, "From here, this is the best seat in the gym!"

Ashlyn held up her cup of punch like a trophy. "To safe listening," she called back, and clinked it against the fire extinguisher.

activity: to solve linear equations with one variable by doing the same operation to both sides
knowledge_domain: to solve linear equations with one variable by doing the same operation to both sides
fact: Some linear equations have no solution, such as x + 1 = x + 2, because no number is one more and two more than itself at once.
story:
Christopher had forty minutes before the community centre's math club ended, and the puzzle on his worksheet still wasn't solved. Solve for x: x + 1 = x + 2. Ms. Dang had written it on the board for anyone who finished early, and Christopher had finished early, which now felt like a trap.

"Take away one from both sides," said Jannah, leaning over from the next desk. "That's what she taught us. Whatever you do to one side, you do to the other."

Christopher wrote it out. Both sides became just x = x + 1. He tried again, taking away an x from each side, and got 1 = 2, which looked even worse. He rubbed his eyes. His brain felt like it was producing some panic hormone that made everything foggy. "Every equation Ms. Dang gave us before had an answer," he said. "Even the hard ones."

"That's why it's a puzzle," said Paisley from across the table, not looking up from her own page. "Maybe the answer is weird."

Christopher tested a few numbers anyway, because guessing was his way of checking an idea. If x was five, then the left side was six and the right side was seven. If x was a hundred, he got one hundred one and one hundred two. If x was zero, he got one and two. Every number he tried came out the same way: the right side was always exactly one bigger. He sat back. No number could be one more and two more than itself at the same time. There wasn't a hidden answer; there was no answer at all.

"There's no solution," he said out loud. "No number works. Ever."

Jannah grabbed her calculator and magnified the problem on the tiny screen by typing in bigger and bigger numbers, millions, then billions, and every time the two sides stayed one apart. "It's true," she said. "I actually believe you. That's credible."

"That's the point," said Ms. Dang, walking past with her keys already in her hand. "Five minutes, everyone. Put your work on the corner of my desk."

Christopher copied his steps neatly, then wrote one more line at the bottom: no number can make this true. On his way to the front, he paused. "Ms. Dang, if one equation can have no answer, how do we know the others aren't tricks too?"

She smiled and glanced at the clock. "Check tomorrow's worksheet. Problem twelve."

Christopher slid his page onto the desk and ran for the door, already planning to get there early.

activity: building a project for the school science fair
knowledge_domain: building a project for the school science fair
fact: In a blind test, participants do not know which sample is which, so their expectations cannot sway their answers.
story:
The automatic doors of Hartley's Hardware sucked open, and Jeremy walked in holding a crumpled list. At the top, in his own handwriting, it said SCIENCE FAIR PROJECT: THE GREAT CEREAL TEST, and below that, in smaller letters, do not mess this up. He needed masking tape, paper bowls, and a marker, because his question was one nobody at lunch could answer honestly: did people actually like the expensive name-brand cereal better, or did they just like the box?

He found the bowls first, stacked on a high shelf, and had to stand on the bottom rack of a rolling cart to retrieve them. The cart rolled. Jeremy rode it two feet before grabbing the shelf, and a man in an orange apron looked over and said, "We don't do rides till after five." Brynlee appeared around the end of the aisle with the tape in her hand and Haylee behind her, giggling.

"Here's the problem," Jeremy said, walking now, pushing the cart. "Yesterday I asked my brother which cereal was better, and he picked the name brand before he even tasted it. He saw the box." He pulled his notebook from his back pocket, careful not to bend the spine, and opened it to his plan. "So I can't just ask people. Their answers are already biased."

Haylee frowned. "Biased how?"

"Like, they already decided the fancy one wins," Jeremy said. In the marker aisle he stopped, thinking. If people saw the boxes, the whole test was useless. He needed a way to hide which bowl was which. Even from himself, maybe. He stared at the marker rack for a long moment, then grabbed a black one. "We put the cereal in plain bowls and label them A and B. Nobody knows which sample is which, so their expectations can't sway their answers. That's called a blind test." Brynlee's eyes went wide, like a light had switched on behind them.

"Wait," she said, "so even you don't know which bowl is the name brand?" Jeremy grinned and wrote BLIND TEST in capital letters across the notebook page. He didn't. He would have Haylee pour the cereal and hide the boxes in a backpack, and she would keep the answer sealed in an envelope until every taster had voted.

At the checkout, the total came to $6.42, which left him twelve dollars of allowance for actual cereal. On the way out, Brynlee spun the marker between her fingers. "My dad is going to be so mad if the store brand wins," she said. "He's loyal to that rooster on the box." Haylee held the door and asked, "So if everyone picks bowl B, and B turns out to be the cheap one, what do we tell them?" Jeremy tucked the receipt into his notebook and said, "We tell them their taste buds aren't fooled by a cartoon rooster."

activity: to improvise a scene with a partner by accepting each offer with yes, and
knowledge_domain: to improvise a scene with a partner by accepting each offer with yes, and
fact: In improv, an offer is anything a performer says or does that gives information about the scene, such as a place, a name or a problem.
story:
Amelia had signed up for the Saturday improv workshop because her mother said it would help her "come out of her shell," which was the kind of thing adults said when they meant "talk more at parties." Either way, she was now standing on the small stage of the community theatre with eleven strangers and one folding chair, wondering which of them would humiliate her first.

Ms. Oliveira clapped twice. "Partner up. Two-person scenes. One rule: when your partner gives you something, take it, and add to it. Yes, and." She said it like it was the only sentence she planned to repeat all day, which it was.

Amelia got paired with Cash, a boy from her science class who wore the same green hoodie every day and once ate a crayon on a dare in sixth grade. Good enough. At least she knew his last name.

They walked out to center stage. Cash rubbed his hands together and mimed shivering, then held his arms out like he was gripping a fishing rod, reeling it in slowly. Amelia, who was busy deciding what her character's job should be, ignored all of it and said, "Hi, I'm a dentist. I have an appointment at three."

There was a pause. Cash kept reeling. The audience of other kids giggled, the way people giggle when two things are happening at once and only one of them is being acknowledged.

"Cash made three offers," Ms. Oliveira said from the front row. "Amelia took zero." She didn't say more than that. She tilted her head at Cash, who was still holding the invisible rod, and waited.

Amelia stared at him. The shivering meant cold, so they were somewhere cold. The rod meant fishing, so they were fishing, probably through ice. He hadn't said a word, and somehow he'd already built half a scene without her. She tried to isolate what exactly she'd missed, and it wasn't the mime itself, she'd seen it. She just hadn't treated it as information. An offer, apparently, was anything a performer said or did that told you something about the scene: a place, a name, a problem. Cash had handed her a frozen lake and a hungry afternoon, and she'd responded with dental hygiene.

She felt a small flare of resentment toward the rule, and toward Cash, and toward the green hoodie. It passed, but she could imagine it turning corrosive if she let it sit, if she spent the rest of the workshop deciding that improv was for loud kids with invisible fishing rods. She exhaled instead.

"Right," she said, and turned back to him. "Sorry. Yes, and. Okay." She dropped to her knees beside him, cupped her hands around her mouth, and peered down at the imaginary hole in the ice. "Yes, and the fish we're trying to catch swallowed my dentist's ring this morning, and if we don't get it back by three, my patient is going to be one very unhappy walrus."

Cash blinked once, then reeled faster. "Then hold on tight, because this one's a fighter."

activity: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
knowledge_domain: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
fact: Diwali, the Hindu festival of lights, is marked by lighting small oil lamps called diyas and is usually celebrated over five days.
story:
Victor balanced the last clay lamp on the window ledge of the cultural center, careful not to tip the oil. His grandmother had sent him over from the craft table with strict instructions: every diya had to be in place before dark. "Why this many?" he asked her, counting. "Forty-eight."

"Diwali runs five days," she said, straightening a wick with her thumb. "So we fill every ledge we can. These little oil lamps are called diyas." She smiled and went back to the kitchen, where volunteers were stacking plates of sweets.

Victor kept thinking about the number as he worked. If there were five days, why was the center only lighting lamps tonight? Maybe, he decided, it had to do with the lamps themselves. He would test it. He lit one diya from the candle Mr. Harper, the center's coordinator, was carrying past, then set it at the far end of the ledge and watched. Ten minutes later it was out, though the ones in the middle still burned. He lit it again, and again it went dark while its neighbors glowed. Something was putting out that one lamp, and only that one.

His friend Francis wandered over from the food line with Ariel, both of them holding paper cups of chai. "Your lamp keeps dying," Francis said. "Bad wick, probably." Victor shook his head. "The wick is fine. Watch." He cupped his hands around the flame, and it steadied. When he pulled them away, it flickered hard toward the room. He placed a strip of cardboard behind the lamp, and the flame sat straight and calm. "It's the door," he said. "Every time it opens, there's a draft, and this lamp is right in line for it." Just then Ariel's little brother burst in, and the door swung shut with an abrupt bang that sent the flame ducking again.

Victor adjusted the whole row, sliding the end lamps a hand's width inward so none sat in the draft's path, then checked each one. All forty-eight burned steadily. Mr. Harper came by with his candle and paused. "Nice work. You know, some of the families here tonight came as refugees from Uganda years ago," he said, nodding toward a group of grandparents by the stage. "They told me once that the first Diwali they celebrated here, half the lamps blew out, and they just kept relighting them. Every night. All five days."

Victor looked down the ledge, at the row of small flames holding steady against the glass, and then at the stage where the drummers were picking up their sticks for the second set. His grandmother appeared beside him with an armful of extra wicks. "Still all lit?" she asked. He grinned. "Every single one," he said. "And I know which one to check first tomorrow."

activity: to build a spreadsheet with a formula that adds a column and makes a bar chart
knowledge_domain: to build a spreadsheet with a formula that adds a column and makes a bar chart
fact: SUM skips cells that hold text, so a number stored as text is silently left out of the total.
story:
Jacob had promised Mr. Kapoor that the spreadsheet for the class fundraiser would be ready by Friday, and by Thursday lunch it almost was. He had one column for each sixth-grade class showing how many canned goods they had collected, and a formula at the bottom: =SUM(B2:B5). Beside him in the computer lab, Marilou leaned over his shoulder.

"It looks good," she said, "but the total is wrong. My class brought forty-two cans and I counted every single one." She pointed at the bar chart, where Class 6B's bar stretched tall and proud but the number above it read 148 instead of 190.

Jacob checked her cell. B3 said 42, right there in plain sight. He pressed Enter on the formula again. Still 148. "The spreadsheet is being rebellious," he muttered, but he didn't actually believe that. Spreadsheets didn't have moods. Something invisible was going on, some rule he couldn't see, and invisible rules made him want to dig.

Rayyan slid his chair over from the next computer. "Try adding them one by one," he suggested, because Rayyan trusted nothing he couldn't watch happen. So Jacob typed =B2+B3+B4+B5 and hit Enter. The answer came up 190.

Jacob sat back. Both formulas used the same numbers, so why did one skip forty-two cans? He clicked on Marilou's cell, the one she had copied from a note a parent had sent, and stared at the formula bar. Then he clicked on his own cells and compared. There had to be a difference, some hidden mark. He tried an experiment: he typed 42 fresh into B3, and the SUM answer jumped to 190. When he pasted the original back, it dropped again.

"That cell isn't really a number," Jacob said slowly. "It just looks like one. It's stored as text, and SUM skips cells that hold text. It just leaves them out and doesn't warn you." He typed an apostrophe before a number in another cell to test it, and sure enough the total shrank again without a single complaint from the program.

Mr. Kapoor walked past and glanced at the screen. "Is the chart working?"

"It is now," Jacob said. He retyped Marilou's number as a true number, and her class bar rose to its proper height, finally as tall as it deserved. Marilou grinned and wrote her own criterion on the whiteboard for next year's class: every total must be checked against a hand count.

"Want to help me teach the fourth graders this next week?" Jacob asked Rayyan. "Somebody has to warn them."

Rayyan was already pulling up a blank spreadsheet. "Then let's make the bars go up first," he said.

activity: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
knowledge_domain: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
fact: Friendships usually fade without contact, so friends who move apart and stay close tend to keep in touch regularly through calls, messages or visits.
story:
Maelie sat on the floor of her nearly empty bedroom with her phone and a notebook, listening to the moving truck rumble in the driveway. Marie and Romie were coming over at noon, before the truck left at two, and Maelie wanted a plan written down before they arrived. She had watched her cousin Kayla lose her best friend after Kayla moved away three summers ago. Nobody fought. Nobody decided anything. They just stopped calling, and by Christmas they were strangers who liked each other's photos.

Maelie flipped to a fresh page and wrote a question at the top: what made the friendships that survived? She could not see the cause directly, so she looked at the ones she knew. Ms. Demetriou, her old teacher, had stayed close with a friend who lived across the country for twenty years, and every time Maelie had visited her classroom after school, Ms. Demetriou was on a video call on Thursday afternoons, same time every week. Her uncle still drove four hours every spring to see his college roommate. The pattern was the same in both: the friends who stayed close kept in touch on a regular schedule, calls or messages or visits, and the ones who drifted apart had done nothing at all. Maelie tested the idea against Kayla. Kayla and her friend had promised to text whenever. Whenever meant never. The pattern held.

When Marie and Romie arrived, Maelie handed them the notebook. "Read the top part," she said. Marie read the question out loud, then the list underneath: Thursday calls, spring visits, the whenever that never happened. "So the probable thing is, we fade without contact," Romie said slowly. "Unless we plan it." Marie pointed at the last line of the page, where Maelie had written a proposal: video call every Sunday at four, one word from each of them every Wednesday, one visit before next summer.

They still had an hour, so they tested the plan on the hardest part, the Wednesday messages. Marie wrote one and Maelie summarized it back to her to prove the messages could carry real information instead of just emojis. Then Romie raised a problem. "What if one of us is busy at four on a Sunday?" They agreed on a rule: whoever missed the call sent a voice message before bedtime, and the others answered by morning. Marie called it the backup rule and made Maelie write it down twice.

At one fifty, the driver leaned on the horn. Romie took a photo of the notebook page so all three of them had the schedule, and Marie made them each recite it once out loud, like a drill, until Maelie called them veterans of a war that had not started yet.

The truck pulled out at two ten. From the front window, Maelie watched until it turned the corner, then opened her phone and typed the first Wednesday word: "honeysuckle." Marie answered in four minutes: "Yours by the fence. Romie says to tell you the call is still on for Sunday."

activity: getting through an evening power cut at home
knowledge_domain: getting through an evening power cut at home
fact: The Northeast blackout that began on August 14, 2003, cut power to about 55 million people in parts of the northeastern United States and Ontario, Canada.
story:
The lights at Grandma's house went out at half past seven, right in the middle of a card game. Avery froze with two cards in her hand while the refrigerator wound down into silence. Grandma felt along the shelf above the stove, found the birthday-candle box, and set a stub of wax in a saucer without any fuss at all, as if she had rehearsed it.

Avery went to the front window. The street outside was black, no porch lights, no glow from the corner store. She remembered something Grandma had said once, about August 14, 2003, when the whole Northeast had gone dark. "The blackout that day cut power to about fifty-five million people," Grandma had said, stirring her tea, "across parts of the northeastern United States and Ontario, Canada. I walked home from work the whole way, and every block was dark." Avery stared out at the street and decided that was happening again, a giant grid going down city by city, and her stomach tightened. She texted her friend Faith: is your power out? Then she tried Ismael. Nothing came back but the spinning wheel, which seemed to prove it. If the towers were down, the phones would be next. She imagined fifty-five million people all staring out dark windows at the same time.

"There's a flashlight in the pantry, behind the flour," Grandma said. "And hand me that knitting, dear. I can do the plain rows by candlelight, but not the intricate ones, the cable pattern needs my good eyes." Her needles started clicking, slow and calm, like a clock.

Avery fetched the flashlight and, on her way back, happened to stand on the second stair, where the window sat higher than the boxwood hedge. The hedge had concealed it all evening, but from this angle she could see straight into the neighbor's kitchen. Their ceiling light was on. Two houses down, a lamp glowed in an upstairs room. The street was not dark after all; only Grandma's side of it was. She changed her mind on the spot and marched to the basement, where the breaker panel waited with its intricate rows of little black switches, each labeled in Grandpa's tidy handwriting. The main switch had flipped to the middle position. She pushed it firmly up.

The refrigerator hummed. The kitchen lights bloomed, and Grandma looked over her glasses at the ceiling. "Well," she said, laying down her needles. "Not fifty-five million after all. Just us." The porch light clicked on outside, and somewhere down the block a dog barked once at the sudden brightness. Avery picked up her phone and found two messages waiting: Faith's said no, why? and Ismael's said, what blackout? She laughed and sat back down at the cards. "Deal," she said.

activity: the idea that prices rise when many people want something scarce and fall when it is plentiful
knowledge_domain: the idea that prices rise when many people want something scarce and fall when it is plentiful
fact: When a price is kept below the equilibrium price, more people want the item than there are items for sale, and economists call that gap a shortage.
story:
The line outside HeatWave Sneakers stretched past the pretzel stand before the mall even opened. Edouard got there at seven with his friend Atlas, both of them bouncing on their toes, because today the store was releasing the Nova Blitz shoes for only forty dollars, which was less than half of what most stores would charge. "Two hundred pairs," the security guard kept saying as he walked up and down. "Two hundred pairs, people, that's all we got."

By eight there were easily six hundred people. Edouard counted them in chunks of ten, using the ceiling tiles above the fountain to magnify his count when the line doubled back on itself and he lost his place. An eccentric man near the front wore a bathrobe and a foam shoe hat, and he'd brought a folding chair and a thermos like he intended to camp there for a week. "Why so cheap?" Edouard asked him. "Why not just charge more?" The man shrugged. "Ask the store. I just know a deal when I see one."

At eight sharp the doors opened, and the crowd surged forward like water through a broken dam. Edouard and Atlas got shoved sideways, and within eleven minutes a clerk hung a sign in the window: SOLD OUT. Behind them, hundreds of people stood holding nothing. On the bench outside, a girl from Edouard's class named Kaydence sat with her arms crossed. "My cousin showed up at six," she said. "Still didn't get a pair. There were way more of us than there were shoes."

Edouard sat down next to her and pulled out the little notebook he used for math class. At the top he wrote "cheap price, 200 shoes, 600 people." He ran a quick analysis in his head, the way Ms. Desir had shown them for word problems, and something clicked. If the shoes had cost a hundred dollars, half these people would have walked away before the doors even opened. The low price was the whole problem. It was like the store had built a dam and then wondered why the river piled up behind it. "Kaydence," he said, "I think there's a word for this." He texted his older sister, who was in high school economics, and she wrote back one word: shortage.

"More people want them than there are shoes," Edouard said, reading it off his phone. "That's what a shortage is." Kaydence grabbed the notebook and drew an arrow from "cheap price" to "shortage" and circled it twice. Atlas pointed at a kid leaving the store with a boxed pair under each arm, walking fast toward the exit. "Where's he going in such a hurry?" The kid called back over his shoulder, "Online, my friends. These just became two hundred dollars each." Edouard looked at the empty window display, then at his notebook, and underlined the word shortage so hard the pencil tore the page.

activity: to play a piece with dynamics and tempo changes in a band or on the piano
knowledge_domain: to play a piece with dynamics and tempo changes in a band or on the piano
fact: Johann Nepomuk Maelzel patented the mechanical metronome, a ticking device that sets a steady tempo, in 1815.
story:
Alexandre had been playing the new piano piece for a week, and he thought he had it nailed. Then Ms. Toussaint crossed the studio, slid a small wooden box toward him, and said, "Play it once more, with this ticking beside you." The box had a pendulum inside and a sliding weight, and it ticked like a patient clock. Alexandre set his hands on the keys, the tick started, and within eight measures he was already ahead of it, charging through the soft passage and scrambling the crescendo.

"That's the plague of my practicing," Alexandre groaned. "I rush everything."

"It's a common plague," Ms. Toussaint agreed, adjusting the weight. "Now listen before you play. Just listen."

He listened. The tick stayed exactly the same, steady as a heartbeat, and it hit him that the machine would never slow down for him or speed up for him. He tried the piece again and matched his fingers to the tick. At the soft part, where the music was supposed to shrink to a whisper, he discovered that he could still keep the same tempo while playing quietly, something he had never managed on his own. "It's like the tempo is invisible and this thing makes it visible," he said.

Ava, who was waiting for her lesson on the couch by the window, leaned forward. "What's it called?"

"A metronome. Ms. Toussaint says Maelzel patented it in 1815." He liked saying the year out loud, because it meant people had been fighting rushing fingers for more than two hundred years, and someone had built a machine to argue back.

"You're grinning like you invented it," Ava said.

"It's just ironic that a ticking box beat me at something I practice an hour a day."

He ran the piece a third time, and this time he added the tempo changes the way the page demanded, slower in the middle section, faster at the finish, always measured against the tick. When he slowed down, he could hear the tick waiting for him, patient and slightly smug, like a rival runner pacing him. When the last chord rang out, the room felt bigger than before.

On the walk home, an idea began to germinate in his head: if he practiced with the metronome every day for two weeks, he could train his internal clock, and by the spring recital he might not need it at all. He could just feel the tempo. He said so to Ava, who was walking beside him with her violin case bumping her knee.

"Two weeks? You said you couldn't live without it a minute ago."

"Watch me," Alexandre said, and he tapped the beat all the way down the block, two steady knocks against his leg for every step.

activity: to solve linear equations with one variable by doing the same operation to both sides
knowledge_domain: to solve linear equations with one variable by doing the same operation to both sides
fact: A word problem can be turned into an equation: if a taxi charges 3 dollars plus 2 dollars per kilometre and a ride costs 15, then 3 + 2k = 15, so k = 6.
story:
The community centre homework club met in the room with the tropical fish, which Rebecca found more tranquil than any of the actual students. She spread out her math sheet, and next to her Albert was building what he claimed was a paper airplane but which looked more like a paper accident. He wanted to enter the launch contest at the centre on Saturday, and so far his best design had flown sideways into the fish tank.

"I need aerodynamics help," Albert said, "but first you need to help me with this." He slid the worksheet across. Ms. Cohen, who ran the club and had recently announced she would retire at the end of the year, was helping someone else, so Rebecca was on her own.

The problem was about a taxi. Rebecca read it twice. A taxi charges 3 dollars plus 2 dollars per kilometre. A ride costs 15 dollars. How far did they travel? She thought of the receipt in her grandmother's kitchen drawer, the one from the hospital trip after her grandmother's concussion last spring, with its mysterious total printed at the bottom. Nobody in the family had ever worked out how far the hospital actually was.

Rebecca wrote 3 + 2k = 15 on her paper. The k was the kilometres, the thing she couldn't see. "It's hiding," she told Albert. "I have to unhide it."

"You sound like the fish are talking to you," said Albert.

She tried something. The 3 was in the way, so she took 3 away from one side. Then, because Ms. Cohen's one rule written on the whiteboard said whatever you do to one side you do to the other, she took 3 from the other side too. That left 2k = 12. She stared at it. Two of something made 12, so one of something made 6. She divided both sides by 2 and got k = 6. Six kilometres. She checked it backward: 3 plus 2 times 6 was 15. It balanced, like a seesaw with equal kids on each end.

"That's it?" Albert said. "You just did the same thing to both sides until the letter confessed?"

"Basically," Rebecca said. She copied the method onto his worksheet where a nearly identical taxi problem waited, then held the pencil over it. "You do this one."

Albert groaned but picked up the pencil. He subtracted 3 from both sides, then divided, then sat back. "Ten," he said. "The answer's ten." He folded his botched airplane into a crane instead, which at least wouldn't hit the tank.

"Six," Rebecca said. "The ride was 6 kilometres. And that's how far the hospital is from my grandmother's house."

She wrote the number in the margin of her notebook, next to a small drawing of a taxi.

activity: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
knowledge_domain: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
fact: A food bank is usually a warehouse that collects and stores large amounts of food, while a food pantry is the local place where people pick up food directly.
story:
The note taped to the library door said the food pantry needed volunteers on Saturday, and Megan had circled it in her head all week. She arrived at nine with her hair tied back and her older brother's work gloves, ready to hand bags of groceries to people. Instead Ms. Ferreira, the librarian, pointed to the book return room, where boxes of cans stood stacked to the window. "Sort those by date," she said, "then we'll transmit the list to the warehouse across town so they know what to send next week." Megan stared. She had assumed the food bank was the warehouse, so she had gone there first, at eight, and found the parking lot empty and the doors locked. No customers anywhere.

She worked on the problem while she sorted. A woman in a truck had finally opened a side door at the warehouse and told her, "Wrong building for picking up. We just store the food here." Megan had thanked her and hurried to the library, but the pieces did not fit yet. If people picked up food somewhere, where was the line? The library had no line either, only Ms. Ferreira stamping books.

Then she noticed the schedule taped inside the pantry closet door: distribution, Tuesdays and Thursdays, four o'clock. Today was Saturday. The pickup happened on other days, at places like this one, and the big building only collected and stored the food until it was needed. "So a food bank is the warehouse," she said slowly, "and a pantry is where people actually come for it." Ms. Ferreira looked up. "Exactly," she said, and went back to her stamping.

At noon Leanna and Hadley wandered in from the farmers market, and Megan put them to work. Hadley wanted to build towers out of the anonymous donation cans, the ones with no name on the label, just a stamped message from someone who wanted no thanks. Megan allowed one tower, then made him take it down. It felt like a small rebellion against the rules, but she was in charge of the closet and she meant to keep it orderly.

By two o'clock the shelves were straight, the oldest cans were in front, and the list for the warehouse was ready to send. Ms. Ferreira pinned it to the corkboard beside the door. "Tuesday you'll see why we do it this way," she said. Megan looked at the empty folding tables that would soon hold bags of rice and pasta, then at the four o'clock line that did not exist yet, and she wrote her name on the Tuesday sign-up sheet in her best handwriting.

activity: to explain how a river carves a canyon over millions of years through erosion and deposition
knowledge_domain: to explain how a river carves a canyon over millions of years through erosion and deposition
fact: In a canyon wall, harder rock layers tend to form steep cliffs and softer layers wear back into gentler slopes, which gives the Grand Canyon its stepped walls.
story:
Bentley had one job on this hike: explain to Mr. Tesfaye how a river could carve a whole canyon over millions of years, and he still didn't have the words for it. The trail climbed along the gorge above Miller Creek, and at the overlook the class stopped while Mr. Tesfaye unpacked his clipboard. "When we reach the quarry face, I want your erosion talk ready," he said. "Two minutes each."

Lilou nudged Bentley's elbow. "You practiced in the mirror, right?"

"Twice," Bentley admitted. "Both times it came out sounding like a book."

Below them the creek ran brown with grit, and Bentley watched it shove sand along its bed. Fine, that part he could say. Water carries stuff, drops it somewhere slower, carries it again. Erosion and deposition. The problem was the wall itself. Across the gorge, the rock rose in bands, and some bands jutted out like shelves while others had worn back into long sloping ledges beneath them, so the whole cliff looked like a giant staircase. Why would rock do that? A canyon was just a river's work, he'd been told, but a river cuts down. It didn't explain steps.

At the quarry face the class spread out along the diagonal path that switchbacked up the slope. Avianna crouched by the lowest band and pressed her thumb into it. The rock crumbled like old chalk. A meter above, the next layer was darker and solid, and it hung out over the soft one like the brim of a hat.

"That's it," Bentley said suddenly.

"That's what?" said Avianna.

"Harder layers form steep cliffs. Softer ones wear back into gentler slopes." He ran his hand along the overhang, then down the smooth slope beneath it. "The soft rock gives up and caves in; the hard rock holds its edge. That's why the walls look stepped. The Grand Canyon must be layered like this, the whole way down." He exhaled, long and slow, like he'd been holding that thought since the overlook. "The river's the antagonist, and the rock is a cast of characters, and some of them fight back."

When his turn came, Bentley stood with his back to the quarry wall so everyone could see the bands behind him. He talked about the creek carrying grit, dropping it where the water slowed, lifting it again in the next flood. Then he pointed at the overhang above Avianna's crumbled thumbprint, and at the long pale slope beneath it. "Millions of years of that," he said, "hard layers standing out as cliffs, soft layers wearing back, step after step, until you get a canyon like a staircase a river built downward."

Mr. Tesfaye made a mark on his clipboard and looked up. "Say the last part again," he said. "Slower."

"Hard rock holds the cliff," Bentley said, grinning. "Soft rock makes the stairs."

activity: playing on a sports team for the season
knowledge_domain: playing on a sports team for the season
fact: Psychologist Bruce Tuckman proposed in 1965 that groups go through stages called forming, storming, norming and performing.
story:
Chloe laced her skates on the cold bench by Rink Two and watched her new teammates argue before practice even started. Nizar wanted the forward line to dump the puck deep. Dhruv wanted to carry it in. They had been teammates for eleven days, and Chloe had been keeping count of the arguments: two on Tuesday, three on Thursday, and already one today about who got the good locker.

"Maybe we're just a bad team," she said to Nizar as they stepped onto the ice.

"That's a contradiction," Nizar said, skating backward. "Yesterday you said we had the most talent in the league."

"Both things can be true," Chloe said. "Talented and terrible. It happens."

That evening she searched on the rink's old library computer while waiting for her ride, typing things like "why do new teams fight so much." She found a psychology page about how groups develop. A psychologist named Bruce Tuckman had proposed in 1965 that groups go through stages. She read them twice, then copied them onto her wristband in marker so she wouldn't forget.

At the next practice she gathered Nizar and Dhruv by the boards. "I figured it out. We're not a bad team. We're a storming team."

"A what?" Dhruv said.

"Tuckman's stages. Forming, storming, norming and performing," Chloe said, reading off her wristband. "First everyone's polite, then everyone fights, then it settles, then you actually play well. We're right in the middle of the storm."

"So we just have to survive each other," Nizar said slowly.

"We have to persist," Chloe said. "And stop treating every disagreement like a war."

Dhruv squinted at her wrist. "Did you write that on your equipment?"

"Mind your own wrist."

The next two weeks were not magic. Dhruv still hogged the puck, and Nizar still yelled about it, but Chloe noticed something small: after one argument, Dhruv actually passed, and after one bad pass, Nizar actually laughed instead of slamming his stick. She kept her tally going anyway. Arguments per practice: three, then two, then one.

Here was the twist she did not expect. When the storming faded, the passing got worse, not better, for a whole session. Everyone was so busy being polite that nobody called for the puck. Chloe skated to the bench, flustered, and found Mr. Quinn, the rink manager, eating soup in his usual spot.

"Your ice is weird today," she said, which was not what she meant at all.

"Ice is fine," Mr. Quinn said. "Zamboni and I had a good talk this morning."

"It's us. We fixed the fighting and now we're boring."

Mr. Quinn slurped his soup thoughtfully. "Hmm."

She skated back out and tried an experiment. At the next scrimmage, she deliberately disagreed with Dhruv about a play, loudly, in front of everyone. He argued back. Nizar jumped in. For ten seconds it felt like the old disaster, and then Dhruv grinned and said, "Fine, your way, but if it fails you owe me a slushie."

The play worked. Chloe got the assist, and everyone screamed like they'd won a championship instead of a Tuesday scrimmage.

Afterward, in the lobby, she bought Dhruv a slushie anyway, because his passing had been beautiful. He looked at the cup, then at her. "This makes my record against you look impoverished. You've bought me three this season."

"Enjoy it," Chloe said. "We're performing now."

Nizar grabbed his helmet and pointed at the door. "Practice again Thursday. Bring the marker, in case we need a refill."

activity: to play a piece with dynamics and tempo changes in a band or on the piano
knowledge_domain: to play a piece with dynamics and tempo changes in a band or on the piano
fact: Pianissimo, written pp, means very soft, and fortissimo, written ff, means very loud.
story:
Aubrey raced up the steps of the community centre two at a time, trumpet case banging against her leg. The winter concert was only three weeks away, and Mr. Taylor had promised the band a real piece this year, one with dynamics and tempo changes, whatever those were. Inside the gym, Liya was already setting up her flute and Quentin was snapping his drumsticks together like castanets.

"Look at the music," Liya said, sliding a folder across the stand. "There are little letters everywhere. P, f, more p's, more f's." Aubrey squinted at the ending of the piece. Two small f's sat under the final bars, and two small p's floated above the last chord. She had no idea what any of it meant, but she decided on one objective for the afternoon: figure out those letters before rehearsal ended.

They played the piece through, and the ending came out like a thunderclap, every instrument blasting at full volume. Mr. Taylor stopped them and tapped his baton on the stand. "That last chord is marked pp," he said, and waited, arms folded, as if he expected them to solve something.

Aubrey stared at the page. The band had played ff, loud as anything, because the ending felt like it should be huge. But the marking said pp, and they had ignored it. She leaned toward Liya. "I think pianissimo, written pp, means very soft," she whispered, "and fortissimo, written ff, means very loud." Liya's eyes went wide. "So we just played the opposite of the whole ending." Quentin, who had been listening from behind his snare drum, held up his sticks. "You want me to whisper with these?"

To isolate the problem, Aubrey suggested they play only the last eight bars, as quietly as they could manage. The first try collapsed into giggles when Liya's flute squeaked, but the second try worked, a soft, shimmering chord that hung in the gym like frost on a window. Mr. Taylor smiled and made them do it twice more. "Now you sound like a band that reads music," he said, "not a band that attacks it."

After rehearsal, the three of them walked out into the cold, already planning. Liya said her aunt ran a bake sale every December and donated the income to the centre, so maybe the concert could raise money for new stands too. Aubrey hugged her trumpet case and grinned. "Soft ending, loud applause," she said. "That's the plan."

activity: to look at onion skin cells under a microscope and label the cell wall, membrane and nucleus
knowledge_domain: to look at onion skin cells under a microscope and label the cell wall, membrane and nucleus
fact: The cell wall is the thick outer border you see around each onion cell, making the cells look like rows of bricks.
story:
Sydney carried the microscope case down to the pond pavilion, where Ms. Navarro had set up folding tables for the outdoor lab. The school's old scopes were supposed to be obsolete, replaced by digital ones with screens, but Ms. Navarro hauled three of the old brass-and-black ones out every spring. "Nothing beats looking with your own eye," she said, which was exactly why Sydney had shown up. Next week was the audition for the regional science team, and everyone trying out had to prepare a slide and label it correctly. She wanted the practice.

Artin was already there, slicing paper-thin layers of onion with a razor and tweezing them onto glass. Remy sat across from him, squinting into her eyepiece and frowning. "Mine looks like a brick wall," Remy said. "I think I broke something. Cells aren't supposed to look like a wall, right?"

Sydney peeled her own sliver of onion skin, dropped on the iodine stain, and pressed the coverslip down the way the manual said, careful not to violate a single step. If the audition judges docked points for sloppy slides, she would dock them on herself first. She clicked through the objective lenses, starting low, hunting for focus. The pond glittered behind them while she turned the fine adjustment, one tiny click at a time.

Then the image sharpened, and she went still. Rows of rectangles, snug against each other, straight-edged and orderly, exactly like a wall. Her stomach dropped for a second. Had she torn the skin? Folded it into stripes? She lifted her head, checked the slide on the stage, and found it lying flat and perfect. So the pattern was in the onion itself, not in any mistake she had made. That was the strange, wonderful part. She bent down again. Every rectangle held a darker dot near its middle, like a small pale moon floating in each brick.

"Remy," Sydney said, "come look at mine. I think your wall isn't a wall. Look at the edges of each brick. That thick outer border, the dark frame around every single one, that's the cell wall. Each rectangle is one whole cell. That's why they look like rows of bricks."

Remy leaned in, then laughed out loud. "So I didn't break anything. My wall is just a bunch of cells standing in line." She grabbed her pencil and started labeling: cell wall along the thick outer border, cell membrane just inside it, nucleus on the dot. Sydney copied the three labels onto her own diagram, double-checking each one against the image, then checked Remy's slide too and found the same brickyard of cells under it.

Ms. Navarro walked past, peered briefly into Sydney's eyepiece, and gave her a thumbs-up without a word. Sydney sat back and looked at the pond, at the water that looked like plain water, and wondered what a drop of it would show under the lens tomorrow. She pulled a clean slide from the box and set it on the table, ready.

activity: breaking an arm and wearing a cast
knowledge_domain: breaking an arm and wearing a cast
fact: As a broken bone heals, the body forms a callus, a mass of cartilage and new bone that bridges the gap between the broken ends.
story:
Max lay on the living room couch with his plastered arm propped on a pillow and a notebook balanced on his chest. Three weeks into the cast, the sharp pain had faded into a deep, itchy ache, and that change bothered him. He had a theory: if the bone was actually knitting itself back together under all that plaster, the ache should follow a pattern, not just drift around randomly. So every evening he recorded where it hurt and how much, on a scale of one to ten, because a single night of notes told you nothing but the cumulative record might.

Noemi arrived after school with her phone and a folding tripod, because she had her own plan. "I'm making a video called Four Weeks in a Cast," she announced, arranging the tripod at the foot of the couch. "Nobody at school has ever narrated their own broken arm before. You talk, I film, and by the end we show everyone what it's really like." She wanted it for the school media club contest, and she had already story-boarded six scenes on graph paper.

Max held up the notebook. "Then start here. I've got data." He narrated the first three weeks for her camera, tracing the ache's path with his good hand. "Week one, sharp jabs right where I landed on the stairs. Week two, the jabs moved outward, like a ring. Week three, it's a dull throb across the whole break." He paused, studying the page. "Something in there is doing something. I just can't see it."

On Thursday he tested his idea the wrong way. Reaching for the remote with his bad arm, he knocked his elbow hard on the end table, and the throb flared back to a sharp jab that lasted two days. His log broke its pattern. He decided the consequence was obvious: he had ruined the healing, reset everything to week one, and he sulked about it until Elsa came over on Saturday with a metallic marker to collect cast signatures.

"You don't know that," Elsa said, printing her name in careful block letters above the spot where the stairs had gotten him. "You guessed a pattern from three data points. In science, that's like, nothing." She wanted her signature to be the first one everyone noticed, so she added a small lightning bolt under the E.

At the follow-up visit on Monday, Max spread his notebook on the exam table and told the doctor everything, including the knock. The doctor clipped the new X-ray to the light box and pointed with a pen. There, over the break, sat a fuzzy gray lump. "See that cloud there?" the doctor said. "That's your callus." Max leaned close. The doctor tapped the lump on the film and added, "A mass of cartilage and new bone that bridges the gap between the broken ends. It means the bone is healing."

Max studied the fuzzy shape, then checked his notebook. The ring of ache, the outward spread, the dull throb, even the flare after the knock. It had all been the callus building itself, invisible the whole time. "It was there the entire time," he said. "My knock didn't reset anything." Outside in the waiting room, Noemi was already rolling, and Max held the X-ray copy up to the light. "Scene seven," he said. "The lump has a name."

activity: persuasion techniques such as bandwagon appeals, loaded words and celebrity testimonials used in ads and propaganda
knowledge_domain: persuasion techniques such as bandwagon appeals, loaded words and celebrity testimonials used in ads and propaganda
fact: A testimonial uses a famous or admired person to endorse something, even though that person may have no special knowledge about it and may be paid.
story:
Camille leaned over the aquarium in Ms. Mwangi's room, tightening the little valve on the air pump so the bubbles slowed to a lazy trickle. Behind her, Darwin dropped into a chair with a magazine and slid it across the table.

"Look at these," he said. A basketball player named Rashad Cole grinned up from the page, lacing a pair of silver-and-orange sneakers. "The GritLine 3. Everybody's getting them. Emerson already has a pair, and half the team says they're the best shoe ever made. Elite. Legendary. That's what the ad says."

"They're a hundred and sixty dollars," Camille said. "That's your whole birthday money plus four weeks of dog-walking."

"I know, but Rashad Cole wears them." Darwin tapped the photo. "If they're good enough for him, they're good enough for me. He wouldn't wear junk."

Camille looked at the tiny print under the picture. She had to tilt the magazine toward the window to read it. "Paid partnership," she said slowly. "Darwin. It says he got paid."

"So? He still wears them."

"Does he?" Camille turned the page and found a smaller ad for a different brand of sneakers, with a different star, also grinning, also lacing them up. Then a third. Three stars, three brands, three claims of legendary greatness. She felt something click into place, like the valve finally seated. "If Rashad thinks one shoe is the best, why does the other guy think a totally different shoe is the best? They can't all be right."

"Maybe they're all good," Darwin said, but he frowned.

Camille flipped back to the tiny print. Paid partnership, again. "It's called a testimonial," she said. "A famous person saying something's great, even if they don't actually know anything about it, and even if they got paid to say it. We did ads in Ms. Mwangi's class last month. Remember the poster with the word 'crucial' on it in huge letters?"

Darwin slumped. "So he might not even like them."

"He might. Or he might just like the money." Camille watched the bubbles rise in the tank, slow and even now, the water calm. "Here's what we could do. Don't buy them yet. Tomorrow, look at everybody's actual shoes at practice. Ask Emerson if his feet hurt. Ask the guys on other teams. Then decide with your own eyes."

Darwin was quiet for a moment. "Emerson's been saying they're durable, but he also said everybody has to get them or you're basically nobody. That part made me feel kind of bad."

"That's them trying to humiliate you into buying," Camille said. "Nobody's nobody because of shoes." She slid the magazine back. "Check feet tomorrow. Report to me."

Darwin grinned and stood. "Field research," he said, and saluted her on his way out the door.

activity: to do a load of laundry from sorting colours to folding
knowledge_domain: to do a load of laundry from sorting colours to folding
fact: A paper tissue left in a pocket breaks apart in the wash and scatters white shreds over every item in the load, which is why pockets are checked before washing.
story:
Ariana stood at the top of the basement stairs with a hamper on her hip, reading the note her mother had taped to the door before her shift upstairs at the bank. "Dark load first. Cold water. Check every pocket. Fold while warm. I'll prioritize the laundry this weekend if it's too much, but you wanted to learn, so learn." Below her, in the little staff room behind the vault, the bank kept an old but durable washer and dryer for the night cleaners, and Mr. Pelletier had said she could use them as long as she was careful.

She dumped the hamper on the folding table and sorted the way her mother had shown her: darks in one pile, whites in another, anything red and suspicious on its own. Inara and Layla had come along, mostly for the vending machine, but Inara was actually helping. Layla sat on the dryer eating cheese crackers and offering commentary.

"You have to check pockets," Inara said, holding up a pair of jeans. "My dad ruined a whole load once."

"Ruined how?" Ariana asked, but she was already halfway through the pile, and she was sure her pockets were empty. She'd emptied them yesterday. Hadn't she? She thought about the grey hoodie, worn all week, the one she'd stuffed with napkins at lunch and tissues during the sneezing fit in math class. She couldn't remember taking them out. That was the thing about pockets, she thought; you couldn't see inside them, so you had to reason from what you'd done, not from what you could see. She checked the hoodie. Two tissues, crumpled soft as clouds.

Layla slid off the dryer. "Okay, that's actually weirdly satisfying."

"Put them in," Ariana said. "And next time I check everything, even the ones I'm sure about."

While the washer filled, Mr. Pelletier came down for his coffee mug and paused at the table. "When my daughter was your age she skipped the pockets once," he said. "One paper tissue, whole load of dark clothes came out speckled white. Every single item." He lifted his mug toward the washer. "Shreds everywhere. That's why we check."

Ariana peeled the two tissues apart and dropped them in the trash, then leaned against the washer and felt it start to tumble. She thought about all the times she'd tossed clothes in at home without looking, and how many speckled loads she might have caused and never known about, and whether her mother had quietly picked white shreds off everyone's shirts and never said a word.

The cycle beeped its long final beep, and Ariana pulled the dark load out warm, laid it flat on the table, and folded each piece while Inara matched the socks. Layla held up a black shirt, turned it toward the light, and said, "Not one white speck on it."

"Two tissues," Ariana said. "That's how close it was."

activity: to chop an onion safely with the claw grip and make a pasta sauce from scratch
knowledge_domain: to chop an onion safely with the claw grip and make a pasta sauce from scratch
fact: Simmering a sauce with the lid off lets water escape as steam, so the sauce slowly gets thicker.
story:
John had signed up for the community kitchen class for one reason: Mr. Buchanan had promised that everyone would leave knowing how to make pasta sauce from scratch. So far John had learned two things. First, that onions could make a thirteen-year-old boy cry like a toddler at a birthday party, and second, that there was a way to hold your fingers so you kept all ten of them.

"Curl your fingertips under, like a claw," said London, who had taken the class twice before and acted like a chef with forty years of experience. "Knuckles guide the knife. Fingers stay out of the blade's way."

John curled his fingers and chopped. The onion halves came out uneven, half cubes and half onion confetti, but all ten fingertips survived. Across the table, Marshall was wiping his eyes with his sleeve and pretending he wasn't. "It's allergies," Marshall said, and John and London both said "Sure it is" at the same time.

By five o'clock the sauce was bubbling on the stove, and Mr. Buchanan set out plates for the families arriving at six. John stirred, tasted, and frowned. The sauce was thin. It slid off his spoon like red water and pooled at the bottom of the bowl. London leaned over and looked too. "Mine's runny as well," she said. "Mr. Buchanan's sauce last week was thick enough to hold a spoon upright. What did we do differently?"

John looked around the kitchen, thinking. Last week's pot had been on the back burner. Theirs was on the front. He walked over to Mr. Buchanan's old pot, still sitting on the back burner, and noticed the lid hanging on its hook beside it, dry and clean. Then he looked at their own pot. The lid was on. It had been on the whole time, since the very first bubble.

He lifted the lid off their pot and stood there a second, watching the steam curl up toward the vent. "The lid," he said. "It's been trapping everything in there. With the lid off, the water gets out as steam, and the sauce gets thicker the longer it cooks." London tilted her head, considering, then found a wooden spoon and propped the lid on the counter, well out of temptation's reach.

They could not postpone dinner, so the six families would just have to wait twenty extra minutes, which Marshall announced to the room like a peasant heralding the king: "The sauce requires patience! Snacks will be served!" Mr. Buchanan, who was spontaneous about very little, calmly sliced bread. By ten past six the sauce clung to the spoon, glossy and slow, and Mr. Buchanan held the spoon upside down over the pot to show the whole room. Nothing fell. Marshall stood on his chair and applauded, and John, grinning, handed him the first plate.

activity: to cook rice, a curry and flatbread so they are all ready at the same time
knowledge_domain: to cook rice, a curry and flatbread so they are all ready at the same time
fact: In the absorption method, rice cooks in a measured amount of water that it soaks up completely, so no water needs to be drained.
story:
Rebecca stood at the camp stove with three pots and a problem. The rice would take twenty minutes, the curry thirty, and the flatbread only five, and somehow all of it had to land on the picnic table at six o'clock sharp, because the whole cabin group would come tramping back from the lake starving and loud. Ms. Wu had handed her a dented pot, a bag of rice, and one sentence: "Tonight you cook, I watch." Then she had sat down on a log with her thermos like it was the best show in the county.

Reem was already at her elbow, measuring rice into a cup with the focus of a scientist. "Two cups," she said. "My mom does it this way, you don't just guess." She leveled the cup with her finger and poured it into the pot. Sebastien crouched by the cooler chopping onions for the curry, sniffling dramatically. "I'm crying," he announced, "but like, in a brave way. This is a robust onion. Possibly two onions in trench coats."

The rice was the puzzle. Rebecca had only ever watched her dad boil pasta in a huge storm of water, then dump it all into a colander in the sink with steam billowing up like a dragon. So when the water in her pot started to bubble, she picked up the pot and swung it toward the sink. "Whoa, whoa," Reem said, grabbing the handle with both hands. "You don't drain it. It's the absorption method. All the water gets soaked up. There's nothing left to pour off." Rebecca frowned at the pot. "All of it? Where does it go?" "Into the rice," Reem said. "That's the whole point."

Rebecca lowered the pot back onto the burner and peered through the steam at the grains swimming around. How could each little grain drink its share, exactly, like tiny camels? She put the lid on and set a timer, and while she waited she worked backward on the rest of the meal, which felt like a math problem she actually wanted to solve. The curry needed thirty minutes, so it went on first. The rice needed twenty, so it went on ten minutes later. The flatbread dough she could mix now and cook last, five minutes in the hot pan. She wrote the schedule in the dirt with a stick, then a mosquito landed on the word "flatbread" and she had to rewrite it.

The middle part was the hard part, because nothing looked like it was happening. The curry burbled and smelled like cumin and coconut, but the rice just sat there under its lid, quiet as a secret. Rebecca lifted the corner of the lid exactly once and a puff of steam rolled up her glasses. "We don't peek," Reem said. "It's like a closed-envelope system." Sebastien, from across the table: "It's like the rice has a constitution and the lid is the law." Rebecca snorted. Fine. No peeling back the lid. But she pressed her ear close and heard the faintest hiss and crackle underneath, like tiny rain on a tiny roof, and she decided that was her evidence. Something was happening in there.

At minute nineteen she started the flatbread, slapping the dough between her palms the way Ms. Wu had shown her until it flopped like a lazy frisbee. The first one hit the pan and blistered up in fat bubbles that she couldn't help but cherish, each one a small triumph of heat and dough. When the timer dinged, she lifted the rice lid and stared. No water. Not a puddle, not a drop. The grains stood there plump and steaming, having somehow swallowed every last bit of it, and she felt like she'd caught a magician pulling off the trick.

The three dishes made it to the table at 6:02, which Sebastien declared "close enough for a first attempt, and honestly the flatbread alone could fix a bad day." The campers descended, and Rebecca watched her pot of rice empty out fast, which was its own kind of proof. Ms. Wu held up a forkful and said, "Same meal tomorrow?" Rebecca was already thinking about whether the timing would change if she doubled the rice, and she said, "Only if I get to figure out the doubling part."

activity: customs such as greetings, gift-giving and table manners that differ between cultures and households
knowledge_domain: customs such as greetings, gift-giving and table manners that differ between cultures and households
fact: In France, friends often greet each other with cheek kisses called 'la bise', and the number of kisses varies from region to region.
story:
Nevaeh had been dreading third period all morning, because third period was when the new girl arrived. The new girl was from France, she had lived in three different cities before her family moved, and Nevaeh had been assigned to show her around. Nevaeh was terrible at meeting people. She usually said "hi" too quietly and then stared at the floor.

The new girl walked into Mr. Rowe's room before the bell, spotted Nevaeh by the science counter, and crossed the room fast. Then, without a word, she leaned in and pressed her cheek against Nevaeh's, once, twice, making a small kiss sound in the air each time.

"Uh," said Nevaeh. Her face went hot. Chanelle, watching from the window seat, mouthed the word weird.

"It's how we say hello," the new girl said. "We call it la bise."

At lunch, things got stranger. Nevaeh brought the new girl to the table where Hayden and Chanelle were already sitting, and the new girl gave each of them the same two kisses. But when Nevaeh picked up her slice of pizza with her hands, the new girl stared, then quietly demonstrated cutting hers with a knife and fork, the way Nevaeh's grandmother did with fried chicken. Fine. Different houses, different rules; Nevaeh's own family thought elbows on the table were a crime. She could live with that.

The mystery came after school. A young man was waiting at the front steps, and the new girl ran to him and hugged him, and then they kissed cheeks three times. Nevaeh counted. She stood behind the mailbox by the flagpole and counted again, in case she'd imagined one. Three.

"So?" Chanelle said, catching up. "Maybe she likes him more than us."

"That's not it." Nevaeh thought about motive the way Mr. Rowe had taught them in the detective story unit. If liking people was the reason, she'd give her cousin three every day. But she'd given two to everyone at lunch, teachers included, without hesitating, like she wasn't deciding anything at all. Which meant the number wasn't about feelings. It was about something else, some rule Nevaeh couldn't see. She had one idea, and it felt almost rebellious to march over and ask a stranger about it, but she did it anyway.

"He's my cousin," the new girl said. "From the south. He'd be lost in Lyon. We do three there, my cousins do, and here at home we always did two." She smiled like the whole thing was the most ordinary fact in the world.

Her cousin offered his hand and a two-cheek hello, so Nevaeh leaned in and carefully gave him back three.

activity: to compare a stock and a bond and explain which is riskier and why
knowledge_domain: to compare a stock and a bond and explain which is riskier and why
fact: When interest rates rise, the prices of existing bonds fall, because buyers can get new bonds that pay more interest.
story:
"Two dollars a basket," said the woman behind the tomato stand, and Jack counted out quarters while Abdullah held the bag and groaned about being used as furniture.

"My mom sent me to find someone," Abdullah said. "A teenager selling a bond. Don't ask why, she's doing some errand thing." He pointed across the market, past the honey jars and a man arguing with a very calm goat, to a folding table with a hand-lettered sign: BOND FOR SALE, PAYING 2 PERCENT, ASKING FULL PRICE.

The teenager at the table, whose name was not on the sign and stayed off it, looked miserable. "Nobody will pay full price," he said. "It's worth full price. It says so on the paper."

Jack picked up the bond and turned it over, as if the back might contain better news. He was supposed to be learning this stuff for a class project with Constance, who was already marching toward them carrying a sack of peaches like a trophy.

"Here's my reasoning," Jack announced. "Constance, you're the bank today."

"I'm the peach vendor."

"You're whatever I need you to be." He held up the bond. "This pays 2 percent. Now pretend the bank, which is Ms. Le's stall over there, is selling brand-new bonds at 3 percent."

Constance squinted at him, then at Ms. Le, who was weighing squash and minding her own business. "Fine. I'm a bank that sells peaches and bonds."

"If you can buy a new bond that pays more interest," Jack said, "why would you pay full price for this old one?"

The teenager slumped. "Because it's already printed?"

Abdullah patted his shoulder with mock solemnity. "The paper does not symbolize the money, my friend. My grandmother taught me that after I tried to pay for ice cream with a drawing of ice cream."

Jack tried a quick test. He walked to Ms. Le's stall and asked, loudly enough to be overheard, "If interest rates go up, what happens to the prices of old bonds?"

"Old bonds get cheaper," Ms. Le said without looking up from her scale. "Everyone wants the new ones that pay more. Eggs are three fifty."

The teenager heard it. He looked at his sign, took out a marker, and crossed out FULL PRICE, writing LOW PRICE instead, with a little frowny face. Two customers wandered over within a minute.

"See?" Jack said. "Rates up, old bond prices down. It's like the inevitable fate of every tomato at closing time. Somebody's going to get a deal."

Constance handed him a peach. "You're buying this. You dragged me into being a bank, and banks get paid." Jack dug into his pocket and came up with one quarter, two bottle caps, and a rubber band. Abdullah tried to pay with the rubber band, and the peach negotiation began again.

activity: the difference between an opinion and a claim that can be checked
knowledge_domain: the difference between an opinion and a claim that can be checked
fact: An opinion supported with evidence is still an opinion, but it is a more convincing one than an opinion given with no reasons.
story:
The group chat lit up at 7:04 p.m., right after dinner. Nylah had typed, "We need a crosswalk on Maple Ave before school. Sign my petition." Aedan replied with seventeen pizza emojis and the words, "We need new cafeteria pizza. Sign MY petition." Elliot lay on his bed with his tablet on his chest, watching the two arguments stack up like rival towers.

"Those aren't the same thing," Nylah wrote. "The crosswalk is a claim. You can check it. I counted twelve near-misses on Maple Ave this month. Twelve kids almost getting hit. The pizza thing is just an opinion." Aedan shot back, "It's a FACT that the pizza is bad." Elliot snorted so hard his tablet slid off his chest and bounced onto the rug. He typed, "Says who?" and Aedan answered, "Says me, a person with taste."
