Elliot scrolled up through the chat. Nylah's messages had numbers, times, and a photo of the corner where the crossing guard's post stood empty every Tuesday. Aedan's messages had exclamation points and one blurry picture of a rectangle that might have been pizza. Elliot tried an experiment. He typed, "Aedan, what would change your mind about the pizza?" Aedan wrote, "Nothing. It's gross." Then Elliot typed, "Nylah, what would change your mind?" and she answered in seconds: "If the near-misses stopped. Then we wouldn't need the crosswalk."

That was the difference, Elliot realized, drumming his fingers on the rug. Nylah's argument was still her opinion, in a way, because a crosswalk was what she thought should happen. But twelve near-misses made it a stronger opinion than Aedan's, which came with no reasons at all, just a flat "it's gross." Elliot typed slowly, spelling it out: "Aedan, an opinion with evidence is still an opinion. But it's more convincing than one with no reasons. Give me one reason. One." The chat went quiet. Then Aedan sent a photo of the cafeteria invoice showing the pizza cost nine dollars a slice and was labeled "peasant bread with cheese product." Below it: "That's my reason."

The next morning Mr. Choi stopped them at the classroom door, holding a printed copy of the petition. "Twelve near-misses," he said, tapping the page. "I was one of them. A driver nearly clipped my bike there last week." He smiled, and the smile turned out to be infectious; even Aedan grinned and added his name under Nylah's thirty-one signatures. At lunch, Aedan slid his untouched pizza slice onto Elliot's tray and said, "Nine dollars. Tell me that's an opinion."

activity: the idea that posts, photos and location data can be stored, shared and seen by strangers
knowledge_domain: the idea that posts, photos and location data can be stored, shared and seen by strangers
fact: Search engines use automated programs called crawlers to copy and index public web pages, so something posted publicly can turn up in search results.
story:
Riley had one job before dinner: find a photo for the class project on migratory birds. He typed his own name into the search box first, mostly because Aleksandar had bet him a fruit roll-up that nothing would come up.

Riley lost the bet in four seconds. Third result down, there it was: a comment on a birdwatching forum, posted when he was eight, signed with his full name. He had forgotten writing it, but there it was, public as a billboard. "Why is it still here?" he asked the empty kitchen. "I wrote that ages ago."

He clicked around the forum and found a page about how the site worked. A short paragraph mentioned that search engines use automated programs called crawlers to copy and index public web pages. So something posted publicly could turn up in search results, even years later. Riley leaned back. Little robot readers, he thought, copying everything they could reach. He wondered how many of them had consumed his comment, carried it off, and filed it somewhere.

Then he noticed the twist. The comment showed his username, but the search result also offered a cached copy of the whole thread, and in that thread, someone had replied with a photo of a park. Riley squinted. He recognized the fence, the crooked bench. It was the park two streets from his house, and the person who posted it had written the date and the time they were there. A stranger, sharing exactly where and when they stood, without seeming to notice.

Riley tested a quick idea. He searched the park's name plus the word "sighting." More posts came up, from different strangers, and a surprising percentage of them mentioned locations: a street corner, a school field, someone's backyard with the house number visible in the photo frame. Each post was harmless on its own. Stacked together, they were a map nobody had meant to draw.

He screenshotted everything for himself, then went to find his dad. "Can you delete my old comment?" he asked. "And can we check what's public about us?"

His dad pulled up a chair. "Let's look."

At school the next morning, Riley found Aleksandar at the lockers. "You owe me a fruit roll-up," Aleksandar said.

"You can keep it," Riley said. "But search your own name tonight. Then ask me about the crawlers."

activity: making an art or craft project
knowledge_domain: making an art or craft project
fact: On drawing pencils, H is usually read as 'hardness' and B as 'blackness', so a 6B pencil makes darker, softer marks than a 4H.
story:
Mia pressed her pencil harder against the paper, but the shading still looked like fog. Her wolf sketch for the community studio's spring show was supposed to be the best thing she'd ever made, and so far the animal looked more like a ghost. Riaan leaned over from the next easel, his own drawing of a soccer ball halfway done.

"Yours is so light," he said. "Are you using a magic eraser instead of a pencil?"

"Very funny." Mia turned her pencil over and squinted at the letters stamped near the end. 4H. She dug through the studio's shared box of pencils and pulled out another one, a 6B, its tip worn soft and round. She remembered the studio's poster had something about these letters, and Riaan had mentioned it once. "H is hardness," she said slowly, "and B is blackness."

"Blackness," Riaan repeated, grinning. "Like a heavy metal band."

Mia dragged the 6B across a corner of scrap paper, and a dark, velvety stripe appeared, like night against the 4H's thin gray whisper. If 4H was hard and pale, then 6B was soft and dark, and that meant she could build her wolf's shadowed fur with the B pencil and save the H for the pale moonlight on its back. It was a radical change to her plan, but she decided to test it on the scrap first: fur strokes in 6B, a few light hatch marks in 4H, side by side. The scrap wolf leg looked alive.

Ms. Murphy came by with a stack of fresh paper for the studio's refugee art class, which met on Thursdays and shared the same big room. She paused at Mia's easel. "That's much stronger than last week's fox," she said. "Whatever you changed, it's working."

"I picked the wrong pencil before," Mia said. "4H for everything. It wouldn't go dark no matter how hard I pushed."

Riaan held up his own pencil, squinting at it. "Mine says 2B. Is that halfway to a heavy metal band?"

Mia laughed and showed him her scrap test, then went back to the wolf. She worked in careful layers, 6B for the deep shadows behind the ears, 4H only where the moon touched the fur. Her hand began to ache, and she shook it out and kept going, because good shading took time to sustain through a whole drawing. When the studio's clock showed closing time, she stepped back. The wolf stood in real darkness now, eyes bright against the deep 6B night. Riaan leaned over, tapped the edge of the paper, and said, "Okay, that one actually looks like it could bite somebody."

activity: to recognise signs of stress and use deep breathing and sleep routines to manage it
knowledge_domain: to recognise signs of stress and use deep breathing and sleep routines to manage it
fact: When the brain senses a threat, the adrenal glands release adrenaline, which makes the heart beat faster and breathing quicker. This is called the fight-or-flight response.
story:
Camille had been practicing the canoe rescue drill all morning, and now her heart was pounding so hard she could feel it in her ears. Her hands shook on the paddle, and her breath came quick and shallow, like she had sprinted up the hill to the dining hall. She crouched on the dock of Camp Birchwater and stared at her fingers. "Myla, do I look sick to you? I feel weird."

Myla squinted at her. "You look fine. Maybe you're just nervous. Musa got like that before the talent show last week, remember? He couldn't even hold the microphone."

That made Camille think. She hadn't felt sick at breakfast, and she hadn't felt sick during warm-ups. The shaky feeling had started the moment Mr. Owusu said her group would perform the drill in front of everyone after lunch. She turned that over while she coiled the rope. Sick didn't wait for announcements. Sick didn't care about audiences. Whatever this was, it did.

She found Musa hauling a bucket of paddles up from the beach and told him about her heart and her shaking hands. He nodded like she'd said something obvious. "That's the fight-or-flight response," he said. "When your brain senses a threat, your adrenal glands release adrenaline, and that makes your heart beat faster and your breathing quicker." He'd read it in a book his aunt gave him, and it was why he'd spent the talent show breathing slowly in the bathroom before he went on stage. It wasn't sickness. It was her body getting ready, like an engine revving.

Camille decided to test it. If quick breathing and a pounding heart meant her brain thought there was a threat, then maybe slow breathing would convince it otherwise. She sat on the dock, planted her feet, and breathed in for four counts and out for six, the way Musa described. After the third round, her heartbeat settled from a drumroll into something steadier. Her hands still trembled a little, but less.

That night, after lights out, she lay awake replaying the afternoon. The drill had gone fine, not perfect, and she wondered whether her breathing had helped or whether she would have calmed down anyway. Last summer she'd hidden in the infirmary during the whole swim test, convinced she was ill, and no one had ever told her otherwise. Maybe she'd wasted that whole day for nothing. She thought about her younger self with an uneasiness she couldn't quite sort out. There was no fixing it now, but there was tomorrow's overnight hike, and the night after that.

She set a plan in her mind, a candidate routine to try: no talking after ten, slow breathing in her sleeping bag, and her flashlight turned away so its beam wouldn't refract off the tent's mesh ceiling and keep her brain awake. In the next tent, Myla was still giggling with someone, the sound warm and infectious even through the canvas. Camille smiled in the dark, breathed out for six counts, and closed her eyes.

activity: the difference between a scientific claim backed by tested evidence and a story about one person's experience
knowledge_domain: the difference between a scientific claim backed by tested evidence and a story about one person's experience
fact: Regression to the mean means unusually bad days tend to be followed by more ordinary ones, so people who try a remedy when symptoms are worst may improve even if it does nothing.
story:
John's grandfather had sworn by his new ginger tea. On Sunday, after two days of what he called the worst headache of his life, he drank a cup and woke up Monday feeling fine. "That tea is a miracle," he told John at breakfast, and he meant to buy three more boxes.

At school, John found Meghan and Stefan cleaning out the crayfish tank in Ms. Hosseini's room before class. Good hygiene in a science classroom meant gloves and fresh water, and Ms. Hosseini had made it clear that anyone who skipped the gloves also skipped the crayfish. John pulled on a pair and said, "Can I ask you guys something weird? If you have your worst headache ever, and then you take something, and the next day you're fine, does that prove the thing worked?"

Stefan shrugged. "It worked for your grandpa. That's proof enough for me."

"It worked for him," Meghan said slowly, rinsing a net. "One person. That's a story, not a claim."

Ms. Hosseini, who had been writing on the board, turned around. "That's the most interesting sentence I've heard all morning. What's the difference, John?"

John stared at the tank. "A claim needs, like, testing? Lots of people, not just one?"

"Tested evidence," Ms. Hosseini agreed. "So how would you test your question? You can't see a headache, and you can't see why it went away. You have to look for a pattern."

That gave John an idea. He asked Stefan to collaborate with him at lunch, and they made a chart. For one week, they asked everyone in their grade who got headaches to rate the pain from one to ten every day, and to write down any remedy they used. They did not tell anyone what to take. By Friday they had thirty-six sheets of paper covered in numbers.

The pattern was hiding in plain sight. People mostly took remedies on their worst days, the nines and tens. And almost every time, the next day was better, whether the remedy was tea, a cold cloth, or nothing at all. Even the kids who just waited usually dropped back to a three or a four. John highlighted the rows in yellow until his marker ran dry.

"There's a name for this," Meghan said on Monday, holding up her tablet. She had looked it up after he told her the results. "Regression to the mean."

"Unusually bad days are usually followed by more ordinary ones," John read over her shoulder, "so people who try a remedy when symptoms are worst may improve even if it does nothing." He copied it into his notebook, then wrote underneath: Grandpa's tea, maybe not a miracle. Maybe just a bad day ending.

He decided to call his grandfather anyway. "Grandpa," he said when the phone picked up, "keep drinking the tea if you like it. But I need to tell you about my experiment."

activity: to build a spreadsheet with a formula that adds a column and makes a bar chart
knowledge_domain: to build a spreadsheet with a formula that adds a column and makes a bar chart
fact: A formula that includes its own cell, such as =SUM(B2:B10) typed into cell B10, is called a circular reference, and Excel warns about it.
story:
Hunter had thirty minutes to finish the spreadsheet project, and the part he dreaded most was still ahead of him: the bar chart. Ms. Zhou had assigned each student a column of fundraiser sales data, and Hunter's job was to add a total and turn the numbers into bars. Landen, two seats over, was already dragging his chart into place with the calm of someone who had done this before.

Hunter remembered last week, when he had tried to build a graph of his Pokemon card collection and ended up with a chart shaped like a staircase to nowhere. He had closed the laptop that day and told himself spreadsheets were invented to punish people. Today he was being slightly less pessimistic, mostly because Ms. Zhou had said the project counted as a test grade.

He typed his sales numbers into column B, rows two through ten. Then he clicked on cell B10, where his last number sat, and typed =SUM(B2:B10), thinking he could put the total right there at the bottom of the list, like a tidy ending. The moment he pressed Enter, a warning box popped onto the screen, announcing a problem with the formula.

"Your computer hates you," Aaden said from across the room, not unkindly.

"It doesn't hate me. It's telling me something." Hunter read the warning again. The word in the message was "circular reference." He said it out loud. "Circular reference."

Landen leaned over. "My cousin got that once. It means the formula includes its own cell. Like adding B10 into a total that lives in B10."

Hunter stared at the screen. His total formula was trying to swallow itself, like a snake eating its own tail. He tested the idea the way he tested everything, by changing one thing and watching what happened. He deleted the formula from B10, put the same =SUM(B2:B10) into B12, one row below the data, and pressed Enter. No warning. The number appeared, correct and ordinary, as if nothing had ever gone wrong.

"Diagnosed and fixed," he announced, feeling like a surgeon who had used a laser instead of a hammer. He selected his data, clicked the chart button, and watched ten honest bars rise up the screen. He dragged the chart beside the numbers and studied it. The tallest bar belonged to the sixth-grade bake sale, which surprised no one.

Ms. Zhou paused behind his desk. "Nice chart, Hunter. And nice recovery."

He saved the file twice, just in case. Then he turned the laptop so Landen could see it. "Look," he said. "Snake, officially un-eaten."

activity: to build a web page with HTML and style it with CSS so the heading is centred
knowledge_domain: to build a web page with HTML and style it with CSS so the heading is centred
fact: CSS uses the American spelling, so the browser ignores text-align: centre; only text-align: center works.
story:
Charlie had typed the same line four times, and the heading still sat at the left edge of the screen like it was glued there.

"Ms. Mokoena said our fan pages have to be finished before the bell," said Yuvraj from the next computer. His page was about the Raptors, and his heading floated neatly in the middle. "Yours is about the Raptors too, right? Copy mine."

"No way. Mine has to be better than yours." Charlie wanted her page to be the one Ms. Mokoena picked to show at assembly, because the winner got to skip the lunchtime homework club and help run the school website instead. She looked at her CSS again. She had written text-align: centre; exactly the way her mother, who painted signs for a bakery, had taught her to spell centre on every menu and birthday banner in the house.

Yuvraj leaned over and squinted. "Weird. Yours looks the same as mine." He compared them line by line, his finger hovering over the screens. "Wait. You wrote centre. I wrote center."

"That's not a real difference," Charlie said, though a small wondering feeling opened in her chest. Could a computer care about one letter? She had learned in science that you have to calibrate your instruments before you trust your measurements, so maybe code was the same: you had to test one small thing at a time and watch what changed.

She deleted the r and the e, swapped them, and typed text-align: center; then hit refresh. The heading slid to the middle of the page like it had been waiting for permission.

"It moved!" Yuvraj grabbed his own screen. "That's so arbitrary. One letter, and the whole computer just ignores you?"

"CSS uses the American spelling," Charlie said slowly, trying the idea out loud. "So the browser just ignores centre. Only center works." She typed centre again on purpose, just to watch the heading flop back to the left, then fixed it. Cause, effect, cause, effect. It was like the experiments they did with plants, except this one answered in half a second.

Ranveer appeared behind them, holding half a granola bar. "Can I borrow someone's page as a template? I spent the whole class on my pictures and forgot the heading."

"Only if I get your crickets for lunch," Yuvraj said. "You always get the good carbohydrates and I get soggy fries."

"Deal." Ranveer sat down and copied Charlie's now-perfect lines, his own page about cricket players taking shape screen by screen.

When Ms. Mokoena walked the rows, she paused at Charlie's monitor. "Centred heading, working image, clean colours. Nicely tested, Charlie. Show the class how you debugged it."

Charlie stood up, typed centre one last time on the projector for everyone to watch the heading drift left, and said, "Now watch this."

activity: to write a Python program that asks for a number and prints whether it is prime
knowledge_domain: to write a Python program that asks for a number and prints whether it is prime
fact: 1 is not a prime number; mathematicians exclude it so that every whole number has only one way to be written as a product of primes.
story:
Annabelle sat cross-legged on her bedroom floor with her laptop balanced on a stack of homework, typing her first real program. The assignment from Mr. Sow's coding club was to write a Python program that asked for a number and printed whether it was prime. She had the loop working, the remainder check working, and a triumphant little "is prime" message ready to go. Across town, Cayson was almost certainly doing the same thing, because he had announced at lunch that he would finish first and demo his program at Thursday's club meeting before she could.

She tested her program slowly, the way a conductor might cue one section of an orchestra at a time. She typed 7 and got "prime." She typed 9 and got "not prime," which felt right. She typed 12, then 13, then 97, and each answer came back correct. Then, just to be thorough, she typed 1, because 1 was small and easy and she expected the machine to breeze past it.

The screen said "prime."

Annabelle frowned. One couldn't be prime, could it? She tried to assess where her reasoning had gone wrong. Her loop started at 2 and checked every possible divisor up to the number itself, and since nothing divided evenly into 1, the program never found a factor, so it printed "prime." The computer had followed her instructions perfectly. The mistake was in her head, not in the loop. She stared at the word on the screen, and it started to look almost ominous, sitting there so confidently, so wrong.

She opened her math notebook and wrote out factor trees to think. 12 broke into 2 times 2 times 3. 30 broke into 2 times 3 times 5. Every number she tried had exactly one way of being written as a product of primes. Then she wrote 1 equals 1, and 1 equals 1 times 1, and 1 times 1 times 1, and the pattern wobbled. If 1 counted as prime, the uniqueness broke, because you could tack on any number of ones and get a new answer. That was it. Mathematicians left 1 out on purpose so that every whole number had only one way of being written as a product of primes. She added one line to her program, an if statement guarding the door, and ran it again.

On Thursday, Cayson went first, just as he had promised, and typed 1 into his own program with a flourish. "Prime," his screen announced. Annabelle raised her hand while the room was still quiet. "One is not prime," she said. "It's excluded so every number has only one way to be written as a product of primes." Mr. Sow turned slowly from the projector and smiled.

activity: building a project for the school science fair
knowledge_domain: building a project for the school science fair
fact: A useful hypothesis must be testable, meaning an experiment could show it is wrong; it is often written as "If... then..."
story:
Olivia spread her poster board across the kitchen table and weighed the corners with mugs. The science fair was in nine days, and her project had a problem: she still had a question instead of a hypothesis. She had written "Music is good for plants" on a napkin, and Ms. Zhao had circled it and written "How would anyone prove you wrong?" in red pen.

Whitney arrived with a bag of sunflower seeds and her own agenda. "I want my name on this," Whitney said, dropping into the chair. "I did the watering last time, and nobody even said thanks." Olivia said that was fine, then held up the napkin. "Ms. Zhao says a hypothesis has to be testable. That means an experiment could actually show it's wrong." Whitney squinted at the napkin. "So 'music is good for plants' is no good because there's no way to break it?" Olivia nodded and picked up a fresh index card.

They tried out wording while eating crackers. "If plants get music," Olivia said slowly, writing, "then they'll grow taller than plants with no music." Whitney read it over her shoulder. "That one you could break. If the music plants come out shorter, you're wrong." They agreed to grow twelve seeds in two groups on the windowsill, identical soil, identical water, one group next to Olivia's speaker playing the same playlist every morning. Whitney labeled the pots W, because she wanted her initial on something permanent, not a temporary scribble on a napkin.

The first four days, nothing sprouted, and Whitney speculated that the seeds were dead. Olivia refused to guess in that direction. "We can't just speculate without anything to look at," she said. "Give them three more days." On day six, five green hooks broke the soil, three of them on the music side. Whitney leaned in so close her breath fogged the window. "It's working. Music wins."

Day nine brought the twist. The tallest sprout, the one Whitney had been measuring every morning with a ruler, was on the quiet side, and by half a centimeter. Whitney stared at the numbers in the log, then closed the notebook. "I wanted music to win," she said. "I even picked the songs." Olivia tapped the index card. "That's the whole point. If the experiment could show we're wrong, then it actually counts when it shows something." Whitney opened the notebook again and wrote the new number down.

By Friday the two quiet-side sprouts had pulled further ahead, and Olivia wrote "Results did not support the hypothesis" on the poster in blue marker. Ms. Zhao stopped at their table at the fair, read the line, and said, "This is my favorite kind of project." Whitney pointed at the W on the pots. "I measured those," she said. "Every single morning."

activity: to use pivot tables in a spreadsheet to summarise survey answers by grade
knowledge_domain: to use pivot tables in a spreadsheet to summarise survey answers by grade
fact: Pito Salas, working on the spreadsheet program Lotus Improv, released in 1991, is credited with inventing the pivot table.
story:
Maeva sat cross-legged on the living room rug with her laptop balanced on the coffee table, a blanket over her knees because the radiator had gone quiet again. On the screen were three hundred and twelve survey answers about cafeteria food, one row per student, with columns for grade, favourite lunch, and whether they'd eat it again. Ms. Gagnon had asked for a summary by grade, and Maeva had promised to have it by Sunday. She'd been dragging cells around for an hour, and the numbers kept sliding into the wrong places like socks in a drawer.

Her dad came through with a mug of tea and stopped behind the couch. "Pivot tables," he said, pointing at a menu at the top of the screen. "Drag your grade column there and your lunch column there, and it counts for you. I remember when those were brand new. Pito Salas invented them, working on a spreadsheet program called Lotus Improv. It came out in 1991, and everyone in my office thought it was magic."

Maeva tried it. Grade went into Rows, favourite lunch into Columns, and a grid bloomed across the screen, every count already correct. "That's it? That's all it does?" It felt almost too easy, like the spreadsheet was doing her homework for her. But when she checked the totals, something was wrong. Grade 8 showed two hundred and four respondents, and there were only about ninety kids in Grade 8. She pulled the blanket tighter and frowned at the numbers. Something invisible was doubling the count, and she meant to find it.

A message popped up from Nassim: "Did you finish?? Brooklynn says the Grade 8s all picked poutine, is that true? Because I don't believe it, they're not that different from us."

Maeva typed back: "My table says poutine won by a landslide in Grade 8 but the count is messed up. Investigating." She decided to decompose the problem: one grade at a time, one row at a time. She filtered the sheet to Grade 8 only and sorted by name, and there it was. Every Grade 8 student appeared twice. The gym teacher had handed out the paper survey on two different days, and half of them had answered twice because they'd forgotten. She deleted the duplicates, counted the unique rows, and rebuilt the pivot. Grade 8 dropped to eighty-nine, and poutine still won, but only by four votes over the synthetic meatballs, which apparently tasted better than they sounded.

She sent Nassim the corrected numbers, then sat back and looked at the grid glowing in the dark room. It had taken one pivot table, one filter, and one stubborn hour to catch a mistake nobody else had noticed. On Monday she'd show Ms. Gagnon both versions, the doubled one and the true one, and explain the difference.

Her dad leaned over the couch again. "So who's the Grade 8 poutine champion?"

"Nobody," Maeva said. "It was a ghost army. I deleted them."

activity: to solve linear equations with one variable by doing the same operation to both sides
knowledge_domain: to solve linear equations with one variable by doing the same operation to both sides
fact: The equals sign was invented by the Welsh mathematician Robert Recorde in 1557, who chose two parallel lines because no two things could be more equal.
story:
Theo sat at the kitchen table with his math book open, pencil hovering over the equation 3x + 5 = 17, and he could not make the x come loose. He had subtracted five from one side once, in class, and Mr. García had circled the mistake in red. "Both sides, Theo," he had written in the margin, and Theo had folded that page away, embarrassed, and never asked about it.

From the living room came the sound of his grandmother's television, too loud, and the smell of onions browning on the stove. She had left a note propped against the fruit bowl before she started cooking, because she never interrupted a simmer at the wrong moment. He unfolded it. "Dear Theo, your mother says you are stuck on the homework. I checked the old dictionary on the shelf, the green one, second drawer of the desk. Look up the short word with two lines. Love, Gran." Below that she had drawn two neat parallel strokes, like the rails of a tiny train track.

Theo found the dictionary and, tucked between its pages, an even older pamphlet about the history of numbers. He read it while the onions hissed. The equals sign was invented by the Welsh mathematician Robert Recorde in 1557, and he had chosen two parallel lines because no two things could be more equal. Theo read the sentence twice. Two lines, the same length, the same distance apart, forever. Recorde had drawn a picture of fairness itself.

"So it's a promise," Theo said out loud. The two sides of 3x + 5 = 17 were equally true, equally heavy, and whatever he did to one side he had to do to the other, or the promise broke. He tested it. Subtract five from the left, subtract five from the right: 3x = 12. Divide both sides by three: x = 4. He checked it by plugging four back in, and it complied, twelve plus five turning into seventeen exactly. The pencil had cramped into his thumb tendon, and he shook his hand out and laughed once, alone, surprised.

His friend Nelly knocked on the door with her own worksheet, wanting help because Mr. García had promised extra credit for whoever could explain why you do the same thing to both sides, and she had only a vague answer that she admitted was not plausible. Theo pushed the pamphlet across the table to her. "Read the middle paragraph," he said. "Then tell me those two lines aren't the best idea anyone ever had."

Nelly ran her finger along the page. "Recorde," she said slowly. "Welsh. 1557." She picked up her pencil, drew two careful parallel lines at the top of her worksheet, and started on the first problem.

activity: to write a short story with correctly punctuated dialogue and a clear climax
knowledge_domain: to write a short story with correctly punctuated dialogue and a clear climax
fact: If a quoted line is a question, the question mark goes inside the quotation marks and the tag after it starts with a lowercase letter, as in "Where are you?" he asked.
story:
Antoine spread his notebook across the library table, next to a stack of books about story writing. His short story was due Friday, and Ms. Morin had written one comment at the top of his draft: "Dialogue needs correct punctuation, and I still can't find your climax." He understood the climax part, sort of. The protagonist of his story, a kid who finds a lost dog, needed one big moment. The punctuation was the mystery.

Lainey dropped into the chair across from him with her own draft. "What's with the frowning?" she asked.

"Commas and quotation marks," Antoine said. "I keep guessing where they go, and Ms. Morin keeps marking it wrong." He slid his paper toward her. His line read: "Where are you going"? He asked.

Lainey tilted her head. "Mine looks different, but I don't know why. It's the most probable reason I got marked down too."

Antoine pulled a published short story from the stack and flipped to a page full of talking. He ran his finger down the lines, hunting for question marks. There, in the middle of the page: "Where did you get that?" she asked. He stared at it. The question mark sat inside the quotation marks, and the word after it, asked, began with a lowercase letter. That felt wrong to him, like starting a sentence with a small letter on purpose. He flipped further and found another: "Are you coming?" he said. Same pattern.

"So the question mark goes inside," he said slowly, "and then he asked has a lowercase h?" He tested it against his own line, which did the opposite. That was probably why the red marks kept appearing. He copied the pattern into his draft: "Where are you going?" he asked. It looked strange and correct at the same time, like a door that opened the wrong way but still led somewhere.

"That has to be the rule," Lainey said. "Ms. Morin will enforce it, whatever it is."

Now Antoine had a different problem, the one Ms. Morin had called the missing climax. His dog story wandered from scene to scene without a peak. He read it over, then took out his pencil and wrote a new middle section where the kid finally spots the dog across a busy street just as the light changes. Then the kid runs. The whole story pointed at that moment now, and the dialogue could carry the ending: "Where have you been?" he asked.

He packed up as the library lights dimmed for closing. At the door, Lainey waved her own paper. "Read mine tomorrow?"

"Only if you check mine," Antoine said, and pushed out into the cold evening with his notebook under his arm.

activity: watching a big game with family and friends
knowledge_domain: watching a big game with family and friends
fact: James Naismith invented basketball in December 1891 at a YMCA training school in Springfield, Massachusetts, using peach baskets as the goals.
story:
The living room smelled like popcorn and salsa, and every seat was taken except the floor. Evelyn sat cross-legged in front of the television with her friend Isobel, while Donald sprawled across the couch between Mr. Sharma, their neighbour, and Evelyn's dad. On the screen, the championship game was tied with two minutes left, and everyone was shouting at once.

During a timeout, Donald pointed at the hoop. "Okay, serious question. Why do we even call it a basket? It's a net. Nobody calls a soccer goal a sock."

"It's just what it's called," Isobel said, reaching for the popcorn.

Evelyn frowned. That answer felt like a door someone had painted shut. Words usually came from somewhere. She thought about it while the announcer read a commercial, and then she pulled her dad's laptop off the coffee table and typed the question into the search bar. "If I can document this, you have to get the next round of snacks," she told Donald.

"Deal," he said. "I'm not scared of a computer."

She scrolled, and the answer appeared in black and white. "It's a basket because the first goals were actual baskets. Peach baskets." She read the rest of the page twice to be sure she had it right. "James Naismith invented basketball in December 1891 at a YMCA training school in Springfield, Massachusetts, and he used peach baskets as the goals."

Donald sat up so fast he nearly knocked over his soda. "Peach baskets? Like, real peaches came in them?"

"That's where the word comes from," Evelyn said. "He nailed them up and the ball had to go in." She turned the laptop so everyone could see the old photograph on the screen, men in wool uniforms standing under wooden peach baskets nailed to a balcony.

Mr. Sharma leaned forward, squinting. "Look at that. No holes in the bottom either. Somebody must have climbed a ladder every time a point was scored."

"Imagine pausing an NBA game so a guy could fetch the ball out of a peach basket," Isobel said, laughing.

The page went on, and Evelyn read quietly for a moment. Naismith had worked with young men who had no income in the cold Massachusetts winter, kids from impoverished neighborhoods with nowhere to go, and the game had given them something to do inside. She thought about her own gym class, rainy days, and the battered ball in the garage. "So the game basically started because a teacher needed something for his students to do indoors," she said.

"He'd faint if he saw this," Donald said, gesturing at the sold-out arena on the TV, the fireworks, the roaring crowd.

The buzzer sounded, the game came back on, and everyone leaned toward the screen. Donald slid off the couch and headed for the kitchen without being asked.

"Snacks!" Isobel called after him. "You lost the bet!"

"Two bags of chips coming up," Donald called back, "but only because of the peach baskets."

activity: words such as anxiety, stress, coping and boundaries used to talk about mental health
knowledge_domain: words such as anxiety, stress, coping and boundaries used to talk about mental health
fact: Mental health includes a person's emotional, psychological and social well-being, according to the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.
story:
The poster outside the gym had been up for three weeks before Alexander actually read it. Mental health includes a person's emotional, psychological and social well-being, it said, according to the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. He read it twice because he was waiting for Robyn, and Robyn was late again.

Robyn had stopped eating lunch at their table on Tuesdays and Thursdays. At first Alexander thought it was a schedule thing, but she was in the cafeteria those days, sitting alone near the windows, headphones in, picking at a pretzel. When he waved, she lifted two fingers and went back to the window. He remembered the fall, before any of this, when Robyn had run the announcements and laughed so hard at Billie's impression of Mr. Clarke that she had to leave the room. That was the Robyn he knew. Something had changed, and the change had been gradual, so gradual he hadn't noticed until it was already done.

He tested his first idea on Wednesday. If it was stress about the science fair, she would talk about the science fair. He sat down across from her and asked how her display board was coming. "Fine," she said, and folded the pretzel bag into a small square, then a smaller one, like it was a ritual she did without thinking. "It's fine." That idea was wrong.

So he stood in the hallway and looked at the poster again. Emotional. Psychological. Social. He tried to work out which one had broken. Not emotional, exactly, because she didn't seem sad when Billie did something dumb in class; her mouth still twitched. Not psychological, or at least not in any way he could check. Social. She was pulling away from people, a little at a time, and nobody had said anything because nobody had a rule for when to say something.

He found Billie at the water fountain and told him about the Tuesdays and Thursdays. "She's coping somehow," Billie said. "Coping means dealing with it, right? That's what my sister's counselor says." Alexander said maybe, but coping alone by a window with headphones seemed different from coping with your friends. He wanted to say it more clearly, but he couldn't paraphrase the poster fast enough, so he just said, "Social is part of it too. Being around people. It counts."

On Thursday he didn't ask about the science fair. He put his tray down across from Robyn and said, "Billie's bringing his telescope Friday. He says Saturn's up. You in?" She looked at him for a long moment, then at the window, then back. "I get anxiety in crowds now," she said. "Even the cafeteria kind." "Then we'll do the roof," Alexander said. "Four people is not a crowd." Robyn unfolded the pretzel bag and folded it once more. "Okay," she said. "Friday."
